title: The wine ran out (John 2:1–11)
hookLine: at a wedding in Cana Mary tells the servants whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye

cards: A village wedding in Galilee. Not an afternoon reception: a feast, guests eating and drinking, the family's honor riding on every cup. Jesus is there, with his first few followers.
His mother is there too. Then, somewhere in the middle of it, the thing a host dreads: the wine runs out. The guests don't know yet.
The bridegroom may not know yet. But someone has noticed. Not the host, not the steward.

teach.b: Mary goes to her son with four words, in the Douay-Rheims: "They have no wine." She doesn't tell him what to do. She just names the need.

teach.h: MY HOUR IS NOT YET COME.
teach.b: His answer sounds cool to our ears: "Woman, what is that to me and to thee? my hour is not yet come." Woman wasn't rude in his language; it's the same word he'll use for her from the cross.
But he's saying: this isn't my moment. Mary doesn't argue. She turns to the servants: "Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye."
Then she steps out of the story.

teach.h: SIX JARS, FILLED TO THE BRIM.
teach.b: Six stone water jars stand there, for the Jewish washing rites, holding two or three measures apiece, John says. A great deal of water. Jesus tells the servants to fill them, and they fill them to the brim.
Draw some out, he says, and take it to the chief steward.
The steward tastes it, doesn't know where it came from, and calls the bridegroom over, puzzled: everyone serves the good wine first, and the cheap stuff once people have had plenty.

teach.h: THE GOOD WINE, KEPT UNTIL NOW.
teach.b: "But thou hast kept the good wine until now." Six jars of it. John calls this the beginning of his signs.

teach.h: WHATSOEVER HE SHALL SAY TO YOU, DO YE.
teach.b: Catholics treasure it for Mary's sake. Her words to the servants are the last John's Gospel gives her, and they point away from herself.
Here Catholics see why they ask Mary to pray for them: she notices the need, brings it to her son, and tells everyone else to listen to him. It's the second Luminous Mystery of the rosary.

how: Catholics pray the wedding at Cana as the second Luminous Mystery of the rosary and often read it at weddings; Mary's words to the servants are a favorite line for describing her role of pointing to her son.

games.q: you're Mary. the wine has run out. you've told your son, and he's said his hour hasn't come. what do you do next?
o: tell the servants to do whatever he tells them.
go and find more wine yourself.
games.why: she turns to the servants: “Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye.” and the water jars are filled.

practice: This week ran from a boy lost for three days, through the hidden years, the voice in the desert, the baptism, forty days hungry and the nets at dawn, to the wine.
Think of the rooms you'll be in today, home, work, a group chat, and look for a need nobody has named: someone running out of patience, money, company or hope.
If you pray, you can do what Mary did and simply say it: they have no wine.

wordCard.voice: Cana. The village in Galilee where Jesus turned water to wine at a wedding, his mother noticing first.

orig.note: Greek: woman, a respectful form of address. Jesus calls his mother this at Cana and again from the cross.

carryVoice: Your line: do whatever he tells you. Next week: healings and encounters. Week five, done.
